newsitem.title: USA: Possible price uptick in 97 not a concern - Phil Fed.
newsitem.headline: Possible price uptick in 97 not a concern - Phil Fed.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia quarterly survey of economic forecasters released on Wednesday showed U.S. inflation is expected to creep up through 1997, but that is unlikely to be a concern, a Philadelphia Fed vice president and economist said.

"In 1996, we had pretty strong increases in food and energy prices and that caused the CPI inflation rate to pick up to a bit above 3.0 percent," Dean Croushore, economist and vice president at the Philadelphia Fed, told Reuters.

"Now in 1997, as both effects get reversed, ... we're seeing early in the year inflation rates of well below 3.0 percent, and then just returning to about the 3.0 percent level. So, in that interpretation, I don't think it's worth worrying about," he added.

The Philadelphia Fed's quarterly survey of 40 economists predicted the U.S. consumer price index to rise 2.5 percent in the first quarter, 2.8 percent in the third quarter and 3.0 percent in the last quarter of the year.

Croushore also said consumer spending was expected to grow between 2.0 and 2.5 percent for the next couple of quarters, and then drop to closer to 2.0 percent in 1998. "That is sort of mirroring the growth of GDP," Croushore said.
The Philadelphia Fed economist also said labor markets were expected to remain tight in 1997.
"It's certainly nice to see that, even though labor markets appear to be tight, inflation hasn't crept up.
"And I think people are forecasting a continuation of the same, that unemployment is not going to rise a lot more ... and we're not going to see a trememdous amount of inflation pressure," he said.
Croushore also said the Philadelphia Fed survey showed economists expected long-term interest rates in the U.S. money market to stay fairly steady throughout the year.
"I think that (forecast) is a combination of pretty steady inflation with ... expectations about some progress on the government budget defict," he said.
"I guess you might interpret that as suggesting that there is not going to be much action in the short run.
"There is not going to be a dramatic action by the Fed, and there are not going to be any other major events in the world that would tend to drive up interest rates," he added.
